procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Assistant Sessions Judge at Sambalpur Sundergarh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 7th October, 1953 of the Orissa High Court at Cuttackin Criminal Appeal No. 108of1952 arising out of the judgment and order dated the 14th November 1952 of the Court of Assistant Sessions Judge at Sambalpur Sundergarh in Sessions Trial No. 7 /4 (5) of 1922.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Orissa High Court at Cuttack heard Criminal Appeal No. 108 of 1952, arising from the judgment and order of the Court of Assistant Sessions Judge. The High Court reached a conclusion (unspecified in the provided text).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Bimbadhar Pradhan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because all contentions raised on behalf of the appellant failed.

issue.issue_text: Whether an alleged illegality or irregularity in the charge, which was not raised before the High Court, could be held to have occasioned a failure of justice under Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellant alleged that there was an illegality or irregularity in the charge.
This specific point regarding the charge was not raised by the appellant when the case was before the High Court.
law: Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states that an error, omission, or irregularity in a charge is not a ground for reversing a conviction unless it has occasioned a failure of justice.
The Explanation to Section 537 is used to determine whether an omission in a charge has occasioned a failure of justice.
application: The Supreme Court found that the provisions of Section 537 were applicable to the case.
The Court specifically noted the fact that the appellant had not raised the issue of the defective charge before the High Court.
The Court then applied the Explanation to Section 537 to this fact.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that because the appellant failed to raise the issue of the alleged illegality or irregularity in the charge before the High Court, it must be concluded, by applying the Explanation to Section 537, that the omission in the charge had not occasioned a failure of justice. Therefore, the argument was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction for conspiracy against one person can be sustained when the only other co-accused is acquitted, especially in light of precedents where it was held that in a charge involving only two conspirators, both must be found guilty or not guilty together.

facts: The appellant was convicted of criminal conspiracy, while his four co-accused in the trial were acquitted.
The prosecution's case involved an approver (a co-conspirator who testified for the prosecution) and other witnesses who were privy to the conspiracy but were not on trial.
law: The Court distinguished precedents where the only alleged conspirators were the ones on trial. In such cases, if all but one are acquitted, the last one cannot be convicted of conspiracy as a person cannot conspire with themselves.
The Court differentiated between English and Indian law regarding 'repugnant' verdicts.

In English law, convicting one conspirator while acquitting the only other in a joint trial is considered a 'repugnancy on the face of the record' and is a procedural ground for annulling the conviction.

In India, the matter is governed by statutory law (the Indian Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code), which has no provision that allows for quashing a conviction solely on the ground of repugnancy on the record.
application: The Court found that the precedent cases did not apply here because, unlike those cases, the conspiracy was not limited to the persons on trial. There was an approver and other witnesses who were also alleged to be part of the conspiracy. Therefore, the acquittal of the appellant's co-accused did not make the conspiracy logically impossible, as he could have conspired with the approver or others.

The Court rejected the argument based on the English rule of 'repugnancy'. It held that this rule is one of practice and procedure in England and is not a part of India's statutory legal framework. Therefore, an apparently contradictory verdict is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to quash a conviction in India.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and upheld the conviction. It reasoned that the acquittal of the only other co-accused did not invalidate the appellant's conspiracy conviction because, firstly, there was evidence of conspiracy with other persons who were not on trial (specifically, an approver). Secondly, the English procedural rule against 'repugnant' verdicts does not apply under India's statutory legal system.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an alleged illegality or irregularity in the charge, which was not raised before the High Court, could be held to have occasioned a failure of justice under Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was entitled to an acquittal because the charge was illegal or irregular, as it omitted the name of the approver as a co-conspirator.
respondent_arguments: The provisions of Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apply. Since the appellant did not raise the point about the alleged illegality in the charge before the High Court, it must be held that the omission had not occasioned a failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a conviction for conspiracy against one person can be sustained when the only other co-accused is acquitted, especially in light of precedents where it was held that in a charge involving only two conspirators, both must be found guilty or not guilty together.
appellant_arguments: Relying on precedent (Topan Das v. State of Bombay), the appellant argued that he was entitled to an acquittal because his co-accused was acquitted. The rule is that where only two persons are charged with conspiracy, one cannot be convicted while the other is acquitted, as a person cannot conspire with himself.
respondent_arguments: The precedent is distinguishable from the current case. In the precedent, the only alleged conspirators were those on trial. In this case, there was evidence of a wider conspiracy between the appellant, the approver, and other sub-overseers who were not on trial. Therefore, the acquittal of the co-accused on trial does not invalidate the appellant's conviction, as he was proven to have conspired with others.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The English law rule that a conviction must be annulled for repugnancy on the record, such as when one alleged conspirator is convicted while all others are acquitted in a joint trial, is a rule of practice and procedure not applicable in India. Under Indian statutory law, such repugnancy is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to quash a conviction for conspiracy.
obiter: The court should not ignore the inconsistency of convicting one person of conspiracy on the same evidence on which another alleged conspirator was acquitted.
The trial court's acquittal of the co-accused in this specific case may not have been well-founded in law or justified by the evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's conviction for conspiracy was upheld because the procedural defect in the charge, namely the omission of the approver's name, did not cause a failure of justice and was not raised in the lower court, thus being cured by Sections 225 and 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Furthermore, the acquittal of his only co-accused on trial did not invalidate his conviction, as the evidence established a broader conspiracy between the appellant, the approver, and other subordinates who were not on trial, making the precedent requiring the acquittal of all conspirators in a two-person charge inapplicable.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 225 and 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an error or omission in a charge is not material unless it has misled the accused or occasioned a failure of justice.

Applying the Explanation to Section 537, if an objection to an alleged illegality or irregularity in the charge is not raised at an earlier stage of the proceedings (e.g., before the High Court), it cannot be held to have occasioned a failure of justice.

The rule that the conviction of one conspirator cannot be sustained if all other co-conspirators are acquitted applies only when the persons placed on trial are the only alleged conspirators. The rule is distinguishable and does not apply if there is evidence that the convicted person conspired with others who were not on trial (such as an approver).
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate how the omission of the approver's name from the conspiracy charge misled him or occasioned a failure of justice, especially since the prosecution's case consistently featured the approver as a central figure.

By not raising the issue of the allegedly defective charge before the High Court, the appellant was barred by the Explanation to Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure from arguing that the omission had occasioned a failure of justice.

The appellant's reliance on the precedent that one cannot be convicted of conspiracy if the only other co-accused is acquitted was misplaced. That precedent was distinguished because, in this case, the conspiracy was not limited to the two individuals on trial; the evidence proved the appellant conspired with the approver and other subordinates.

The court noted that the acquittal of the co-accused by the trial court was on grounds of 'benefit of the doubt' which 'may not bear scrutiny,' implying the acquittal itself was not a firm declaration of innocence that would create a logical contradiction with the appellant's conviction.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the provisions of Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applied, and because the appellant did not raise the point about the charge before the High Court, it must be held that the omission had not occasioned a failure of justice.

The respondent successfully distinguished the precedent cited by the appellant by showing that the conspiracy in this case was wider than just the two accused on trial. The court accepted that 'in that case the only persons alleged to have been guilty of the offence of conspiracy were the persons placed on trial. There was no allegation nor any evidence forthcoming that any other persons were, though not placed on trial, concerned with the crime,' which was not the situation here.
policy_considerations: The court explicitly rejected the English common law rule that a 'repugnancy or contradiction on the face of the record' is, by itself, a ground for annulling a conviction. It held that the Indian legal system is governed by statute, stating, 'In India there is no provision in the statutory law justifying an interference with a conviction on the ground of repugnancy in the record.'

The court affirmed the principle that substantive justice should not be defeated by technical procedural errors that do not cause actual prejudice to the accused, which is the underlying policy of Sections 225 and 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
